description: This topic examines how colonial powers obtained and controlled African labour for the colonial economy, the types and methods of labour exploitation, the working conditions, and African reactions to these policies.

mcq.questionText: Which type of labour involved Africans being compelled to work without their consent and usually without pay?
mcq.explanation: Forced labour was work that Africans were compelled to do against their will, often without proper payment, to serve the colonial economy.

mcq.questionText: Which tax was directly aimed at forcing African men to seek wage employment by charging money for each dwelling?
mcq.explanation: The hut tax required every household to pay money, forcing Africans to look for paid work since they needed cash to pay it.

mcq.questionText: The kipande system in colonial East Africa was mainly a form of:
mcq.explanation: The kipande was a registration document that recorded a worker's details and employment, used to control and monitor African labourers.

mcq.questionText: Which crop was most associated with large plantation labour in colonial Tanganyika?
mcq.explanation: Sisal plantations were major employers of African labour in colonial Tanganyika, especially along the coast and Tanga region.

mcq.questionText: Land alienation forced Africans into wage labour because it:

options.text: Took away land Africans depended on for farming

mcq.explanation: By taking African land for settlers and plantations, colonialists left Africans with too little land to survive on, pushing them to work for wages.

mcq.questionText: Migrant labour in colonial Africa refers to workers who:

options.text: Travelled far from their home areas to work
Worked only on their own family farms
Were employed only in towns where they were born

mcq.explanation: Migrant labourers moved away from their home districts, often for long periods, to work on plantations, mines or settler farms.

mcq.questionText: Pass laws and by-laws helped colonialists obtain labour by:

options.text: Allowing free movement of all Africans
Restricting African movement and forcing them to carry documents
Giving Africans the right to vote

mcq.explanation: Pass laws controlled where Africans could go and required documents, making it easier to channel and discipline workers for colonial employers.

mcq.questionText: Colonial employers kept African wages very low mainly in order to:
mcq.explanation: Low wages reduced the costs of production and increased the profits of plantation owners, settlers and mining companies.

mcq.questionText: A 'go-slow' as a form of African worker reaction means workers:
mcq.explanation: In a go-slow, workers reduced their work pace on purpose to protest poor conditions without openly striking.

mcq.questionText: Contract labour usually bound an African worker to:

options.text: Work for a fixed period agreed in advance
Work only one day per month
Own the plantation after one year
Choose any employer at any time

mcq.explanation: Contract labour tied a worker to an employer for a set length of time, and leaving early was often punished.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following was a common living condition for migrant workers on plantations?

options.text: Free private hospitals for each worker

mcq.explanation: Workers often lived in overcrowded camps with poor housing, sanitation and food, which caused disease and suffering.

mcq.questionText: Desertion by African workers refers to:

options.text: Workers running away from their employment

mcq.explanation: Desertion meant secretly leaving the workplace before the contract ended, a common protest against harsh conditions and low pay.

mcq.questionText: Requiring Africans to grow cash crops for sale was a labour policy because it:

options.text: Forced Africans to produce for the colonial market and obtain cash

mcq.explanation: Compulsory cash-crop growing tied African labour to the colonial economy and provided crops for export while forcing peasants to earn money.

mcq.questionText: A major effect of migrant labour on African families was:

options.text: Separation of men from their families for long periods

mcq.explanation: Because men travelled far to work, families were divided and women were left to manage farms and children alone.

mcq.questionText: Communal or compulsory labour under colonialism was often used to:

options.text: Build roads, railways and other public works without fair pay

mcq.explanation: Colonial governments forced whole communities to provide unpaid or poorly paid labour for infrastructure such as roads and railways.

fib.questionText: The tax charged on every house to force Africans into wage labour was called the _____ tax.
fib.explanation: The hut tax was levied on each dwelling, compelling Africans to find paid work to earn the cash needed to pay it.

fib.questionText: A tax charged on each adult person regardless of property was known as the _____ tax.
fib.explanation: The poll tax was charged per individual adult and was another method of pushing Africans into wage employment.

fib.questionText: The registration document used to identify and control workers in colonial East Africa was the _____.
fib.explanation: The kipande recorded a worker's details and was used to monitor and discipline African labourers.

fib.questionText: Taking away African land for settlers and plantations is called land _____.
fib.explanation: Land alienation deprived Africans of their farms, forcing them to seek wages on colonial enterprises.

fib.questionText: Workers who travelled far from their homes to seek employment are called _____ labourers.
fib.explanation: Migrant labourers left their home areas, often for plantations or mines, returning only after long periods.

fib.questionText: The crop grown on large plantations that employed many workers in coastal Tanganyika was _____.
fib.explanation: Sisal plantations were major employers of African labour in colonial Tanganyika.

fib.questionText: When workers secretly ran away from their employment before completing the contract, this was called _____.
fib.explanation: Desertion was a common protest where workers abandoned harsh and poorly paid jobs.

fib.questionText: Laws that restricted the movement of Africans and required them to carry documents were called _____ laws.
fib.explanation: Pass laws controlled African movement and helped colonialists direct and discipline labour.

fib.questionText: A form of protest where workers stopped work together to demand better conditions is called a _____.
fib.explanation: Strikes were organised stoppages of work used by African workers to press for higher wages or improved conditions.

fib.questionText: Labour in which Africans were compelled to work against their will, often without pay, is known as _____ labour.
fib.explanation: Forced labour was a key colonial method of obtaining workers for the colonial economy without their consent.

tf.questionText: The hut tax was introduced partly to force Africans to enter wage employment.
tf.explanation: Africans needed cash to pay the hut tax, which pushed them to seek paid work on colonial enterprises.

tf.questionText: Land alienation gave Africans more land for their own farming.
tf.explanation: Land alienation took land away from Africans, leaving them with too little to survive and forcing them into wage labour.

tf.questionText: The kipande system was used to register and control African workers.
tf.explanation: The kipande recorded worker details and was a tool of labour control in colonial East Africa.

tf.questionText: Colonial employers generally paid African workers high wages.
tf.explanation: Wages were kept very low to maximise the profits of settlers, plantation owners and mining companies.

tf.questionText: Migrant labour often separated men from their families for long periods.
tf.explanation: Men travelling to distant workplaces left families divided, with women managing farms and children alone.

tf.questionText: Sisal plantations in Tanganyika were known for employing very few African workers.
tf.explanation: Sisal plantations were among the largest employers of African labour in colonial Tanganyika.

tf.questionText: A go-slow was a form of worker protest in which Africans deliberately worked slowly.
tf.explanation: Workers used go-slows to protest poor conditions by reducing their pace of work.

tf.questionText: Colonial labour policies helped develop rural African areas economically.
tf.explanation: By draining able-bodied workers away, labour policies contributed to the underdevelopment of rural areas.

tf.questionText: Compulsory communal labour was sometimes used to build colonial roads and railways.
tf.explanation: Whole communities were forced to provide unpaid or poorly paid labour for public works.

tf.questionText: Desertion and strikes were ways Africans reacted against labour exploitation.
tf.explanation: Africans resisted harsh labour conditions through desertion, strikes and go-slows.

summary.questionText: Name three types of labour used in colonial Africa.
summary.correctAnswer: Forced labour, migrant labour and contract labour (also communal/compulsory labour).
summary.explanation: Colonialists used several labour forms, including forced, migrant, contract and communal labour, to serve the colonial economy.

summary.questionText: How did taxation force Africans into wage labour?
summary.correctAnswer: Taxes such as hut tax and poll tax had to be paid in cash, so Africans had to seek paid work to earn the money.
summary.explanation: Because taxes were payable only in money, Africans were compelled to enter wage employment to obtain cash.

summary.questionText: Explain how land alienation pushed Africans into wage labour.
summary.correctAnswer: By taking African land, colonialists left people with too little land to live on, forcing them to work for wages.
summary.explanation: Loss of farming land removed Africans' independent means of survival, making wage labour necessary.

summary.questionText: What was the purpose of the kipande system?
summary.correctAnswer: To register, identify and control African workers and monitor their employment.
summary.explanation: The kipande recorded worker details and helped colonialists discipline and track labourers.

summary.questionText: Describe the working and living conditions of African plantation workers.
summary.correctAnswer: They worked long hours for low pay and lived in crowded camps with poor housing, food and sanitation.
summary.explanation: Harsh work, low wages and poor camps led to suffering and disease among workers.

summary.questionText: Give two methods colonialists used to force Africans into wage labour besides taxation.
summary.correctAnswer: Land alienation and pass laws/by-laws (also low wages and compulsory cash-crop growing).
summary.explanation: Apart from taxes, colonialists used land alienation, pass laws and forced cash-crop production to obtain labour.

summary.questionText: State two effects of colonial labour policies on African societies.
summary.correctAnswer: Disruption of families through migration and underdevelopment of rural areas.
summary.explanation: Labour migration split families and drained workers from villages, weakening rural production.

summary.questionText: Name three ways Africans reacted to labour exploitation.
summary.explanation: Africans resisted poor conditions through running away, stopping work and working slowly.

summary.questionText: Why did colonial employers keep African wages low?
summary.correctAnswer: To reduce production costs and increase their profits.
summary.explanation: Low wages cut costs for settlers and companies, raising their profit margins.

summary.questionText: Give one Tanzanian example of a colonial enterprise that relied heavily on African labour.
summary.correctAnswer: The sisal plantations of Tanga and the coastal region (also mines and settler farms).
summary.explanation: Sisal plantations, mines and settler farms in Tanganyika depended on large numbers of African workers.

hoq.questionText: Why can taxation, land alienation and low wages be seen as parts of one connected colonial strategy rather than separate policies?

options.text: They were unrelated accidents of colonial rule
They worked together to remove African economic independence and force people into cheap wage labour
They were designed to make Africans wealthy landowners
They aimed only to raise government revenue with no effect on labour

hoq.explanation: Each policy removed a means of African self-sufficiency; together they trapped Africans into providing cheap labour for the colonial economy.

hoq.questionText: How did colonial migrant labour contribute to the long-term underdevelopment of African rural areas?

options.text: It increased food production in the villages
It removed able-bodied workers, weakening farming and local development in home areas
It brought modern factories to every village
It encouraged men to stay and invest at home

hoq.explanation: By drawing strong workers to plantations and mines, migrant labour drained rural areas of productive labour, holding back local agriculture and development.

hoq.questionText: Why were forms of resistance such as desertion and go-slows often more common than open strikes during early colonial rule?

options.text: Workers were satisfied with their conditions
Harsh colonial laws and punishment made organised open protest dangerous, so workers used quieter methods
Employers encouraged strikes to raise wages
There were no grievances among the workers

hoq.explanation: Severe controls and punishments made open strikes risky, so workers relied on less visible resistance like desertion and go-slows.
